In \(R[t]\), \(1+t\) is not a unit, by the same degree argument as in part 4. Thus it does not define that branch *isomorphism* everywhere on the affine parameter line. It does define it on
\[
                         \operatorname{Spec}R[t,(1+t)^{-1}] .
                         \tag{NAX8}
\]
This is the open corresponding to the multiplicative coordinate \(\lambda\ne0\). The distinction is between a valid formal substitution and a claimed globally valid polynomial parameter, not a failure of the proved algebraization over the complete ring.

7. All degree-zero rigidified lines are the gluing units \(R^\times\), by NC's full-family construction for the constant curve. Reduction gives
\[
           1\to 1+\pi R\to R^\times\to k^\times\to1 .
           \tag{NAX9}
\]
Writing a unit in the kernel as \(1+x\) gives the law \(x+y+xy\) on \(\pi R\). The field's multiplicative group is cyclic of order \(q-1\), by the finite-field proof in Lesson 1. Its \(n\)-torsion therefore has order \(\gcd(n,q-1)\). Each such root is a constant element of \(k^\times\subset k[[\pi]]^\times\), and is already an actual \(n\)-torsion lift. NA6 proves that this lift is unique. Thus the model has exactly \(\gcd(n,q-1)\) such lines, all constant in the gluing coordinate. The inclusion \(k\subset R\) is part of this equal-characteristic example, rather than an assumed mixed-characteristic coefficient field.

8. In the fraction field \(t=(tq)/q\), and
\[
                            w^2=1+4(t^2-t)=1+4q .
                            \tag{NAX10}
\]
At the node this is a unit, as its residue is \(1\). The monic equations for \(w\) and \(w^{-1}\) are
\[
                    Z^2-(1+4q)=0,\qquad
                    Z^2-(1+4q)^{-1}=0 .
                    \tag{NAX11}
\]
They prove integrality of both. A function in the node local ring has equal values at the two normalization branches: its numerator has equal values at \(0,1\), and a denominator outside the node ideal has the same nonzero value at both. But \(w\) has branch values \(1,-1\), different in the stated characteristic. Thus \(w\) is not in that local ring. If \(w^{-1}\) were in it, multiplication by its unit \(w^2\) would put \(w\) there too, a contradiction. This shows that the integral-root argument in NA7 really uses normality. It does not by itself construct a global model torsion line that is generically trivial.

9. Here \(b=3\), \(r=3-2+1=2\), and \(g=5\). Hence
\[
                   \operatorname{rank}T_\ell G=8,\qquad
                   \operatorname{rank}T_\ell J_K=10,\qquad
                   \operatorname{rank}(T_\ell J_K/T_\ell G)=2 .
                   \tag{NAX12}
\]
If \(\ell^2t\) is the lift of \(s\), then at level \(m+2\) the transition identity gives \(t_m=\operatorname{lift}(s_{m+2})\) as a geometric generic point. That model lift is generically killed by \(\ell^m\); NA7 kills its \(\ell^m\)-multiple on the model as well. It is consequently already model \(\ell^m\)-torsion. Its closed class \(u_m\) lifts to \(t_m\), and generic injectivity makes the \(u_m\) compatible. Thus \(t\) belongs to the image. Without this argument an injection could have a torsion quotient: the inclusion \(\ell\mathbf Z_\ell\subset\mathbf Z_\ell\) is an injection of free rank-one modules and has quotient \(\mathbf Z/\ell\). The levelwise model argument proves the stronger saturated conclusion.

10. Now \(g=2\), and the two Tate ranks are \(3\) and \(4\). At order \(3^2=9\), the special group has \(9^3\) points over the algebraically closed residue field. Its unique model lifts form a subgroup of the full generic geometric torsion, which has \(9^4\) points. Numerically,
\[
                            9^3=729,\qquad 9^4=6561,\qquad
                            6561/729=9 .
                            \tag{NAX13}
\]
The Tate quotient is free of rank one by NA8. To compare its reduction with this finite-level quotient, NC7 makes projection of \(T_\ell G\) onto \(G[\ell^m]\) onto: choose successive lifts along the onto torsion transitions. CU9 gives the same statement for the generic Jacobian. A basis of the free Tate quotient can be lifted abstractly, giving a direct sum of free modules. Reducing that sum modulo \(\ell^m\) identifies the quotient of the finite-level torsion by the lifted special torsion with \(\mathbf Z/\ell^m\). In particular its order here is \(9\), as computed directly.

The Tate inclusion has different ranks, so its quotient is infinite and it has no finite lattice index. The finite ratio in (NAX13) measures a finite-level quotient, rather than an index of full lattices in one rational space. To interpret the rank-one quotient as a period direction one still needs an actual semiabelian integral extension, a genuine analytic covering and its kernel, finite-extension lifting and local-covering properties, compatible finite actions, and the resulting period valuation pairing. The supplied projective normal model must itself be constructed in the general theorem. NA1–NA8 supplies actual line algebraization and a saturated generic Tate submodule under those stated hypotheses; it has not replaced the remaining constructions.

### 2S. Projective closure and resolution of a supplied nodal model

There are two different geometric tasks here: obtaining a model, and arranging the shape of its special fibre. We construct a projective flat closure of an embedded generic curve. We then resolve a model whose nodes already have the explicitly supplied charts below. The missing step in general semistable reduction is producing those nodal charts after a finite extension.

Throughout, \(R\) is a discrete valuation ring, \(\pi\) a uniformizer, \(K\) its fraction field and \(k\) its residue field. Completeness is required only when we subsequently apply §2R. The elementary free comparisons are the Stacks project's [affine blowup algebras](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/052P), [blowup construction](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01OF), and [nodal chart calculation](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CDC). All constructions used here are proved below.

#### 2S.1. A flat projective closure with a supplied section

**NS1.** Suppose \(C\subset\mathbf P^N_K\) is a smooth geometrically integral projective curve with homogeneous ideal \(J_K\). There is an integral flat projective finitely presented \(R\)-scheme \(\mathcal C\), with this generic fibre and embedding, obtained by contracting the equations:
\[
 J=J_K\cap R[X_0,\ldots,X_N],\qquad
 \mathcal C=V_+(J)\subset\mathbf P^N_R.
 \tag{NS1}
\]
Every supplied \(P\in C(K)\) extends uniquely to a section of this closure.

*Proof.* The polynomial ring is Noetherian by Lesson 3, N1–N2, so the homogeneous ideal \(J\) has finitely many homogeneous generators. On a nonempty standard affine chart the quotient coordinate ring injects into the coordinate ring of the generic curve. Indeed, homogenizing a polynomial relation on that chart shows that it lies in the contracted ideal if it vanishes generically; powers of the chart coordinate clear the denominators. Conversely, extension to \(K\) recovers \(J_K\), because a finite collection of coefficients has a common nonzero denominator in \(R\). Thus the generic fibre is exactly \(C\).

These chart rings are domains and contain \(R\); their generic opens are dense and belong to the same integral generic curve. Hence the charts glue to an integral scheme, and multiplication by \(\pi\) is injective in every chart. A torsion-free \(R\)-module is flat: its finitely generated submodules are free by Lesson 1, §0A; they form a directed union. Tensor products commute with this union, since every tensor and every relation uses finitely many elements. An element in the kernel of a tensor-specialized injection is therefore detected at a finite free stage, and is zero at a later such stage. This proves flatness without a finiteness assumption on the module. Apply it to each chart ring.

Write \(P=[a_0:\cdots:a_N]\). Scale its coordinates so that all \(a_i\in R\) and at least one is a unit, using the minimum of their valuations. They define an \(R\)-point of projective space. All equations in \(J\) vanish there, since their values vanish in \(K\) and \(R\hookrightarrow K\). This gives the section. For uniqueness, two such sections agree generically; the projective-space diagonal is closed, being defined by the cross products \(a_i b_j-a_j b_i\). These products vanish already over \(R\), so the sections agree. This proves the assertion. It proves no regularity or nodality of the special fibre. \(\square\)

#### 2S.2. Constructing the projective blowup and its universal property

**NS2.** Let \(X/R\) be integral, Noetherian and projective, and let \(I\subset\mathcal O_X\) be a nonzero coherent ideal. There is a projective modification \(b:X'\to X\), an isomorphism off \(V(I)\), with the following affine charts:
\[
 b^{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}B)
   =\bigcup_{a\in\{a_1,\ldots,a_s\},\ a\ne0}
       \operatorname{Spec}B[I/a],\qquad
 B[I/a]\subset\operatorname{Frac}B,
 \tag{NS2}
\]
where \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\) generate \(I\) on the chart. Its pullback ideal is invertible and is an effective Cartier ideal. It is universal for this property, commutes with flat base change, and has unique lifts of automorphisms preserving \(I\). If the centre is vertical, \(X'\) has the same generic fibre as \(X\) and is flat over \(R\).

*Proof.* Choose a projective embedding and write \(H=\mathcal O_X(1)\). By Lesson 3, PF7, some \(I(d)=I\otimes H^d\) has finitely many global generators \(s_1,\ldots,s_s\). Off \(V(I)\) they give a morphism to \(\mathbf P^{s-1}_R\). Take the scheme-theoretic closure of its graph in \(X\times_R\mathbf P^{s-1}_R\). This product is projective: the Segre coordinates \(Z_{ij}=X_iY_j\) give a closed embedding, with equations \(Z_{ij}Z_{ab}=Z_{ib}Z_{aj}\). On each open \(Z_{ab}\ne0\), these equations reconstruct the two affine coordinate lists and their products. These inverses verify the embedding on a cover, including rings with nilpotents.

Trivialize \(H^d\) on an affine open and write \(s_i=a_i\). In the projective chart indexed by a nonzero \(a_j\), the graph closure has coordinate ring equal to the image of
\[
 B[T_i:i\ne j]\longrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}B,\qquad
 T_i\longmapsto a_i/a_j.
 \tag{NS3}
\]
Indeed its kernel consists precisely of equations vanishing on the dense graph. This image is \(B[I/a_j]\). A zero \(a_j\) contributes an empty chart. On a nonempty chart, \(IB[I/a_j]=a_jB[I/a_j]\) and \(a_j\) is a nonzerodivisor. Away from the centre some \(a_j\) is already a unit, and that chart is unchanged.

Suppose \(f:Y\to X\) has \(I\mathcal O_Y\) locally generated by a nonzerodivisor \(t\). Write \(f(a_i)=t c_i\). The \(c_i\) generate the unit ideal: the \(a_i\) generate \((t)\), and \(t\) can be cancelled. On the opens where \(c_j\) is a unit, send \(a_i/a_j\) to \(c_i/c_j\). Every relation in (NS3), after multiplication by a power of \(a_j\), is a relation in \(B\); its pullback is zero, and cancellation of \(t c_j\) proves the original relation. This defines and glues the map \(Y\to X'\). It is unique: every ratio must satisfy that same identity, and cancellation makes its value unique on the indicated opens. Thus the construction is independent of generators and embeddings. An automorphism preserving \(I\) lifts by this property; its inverse and all composition identities lift uniquely as well.

Here is the required flat-base-change argument, including when the new ring is not a domain. The chart in (NS2) is the direct limit of \(R\)-modules \(I^n\), with transition multiplication by \(a\), and the multiplication of fractions supplies its algebra structure. If \(B\to D\) is flat, the inclusions \(I^n\subset B\) remain injective after tensoring, with images \((ID)^n\). Tensoring the direct limit gives the algebra of fractions
\[
 (f/a^n)=(g/a^m)
 \ \Longleftrightarrow\
 a^q(a^m f-a^n g)=0\text{ for some }q\ge0.
 \tag{NS4}
\]
The identifications respect overlap localizations, so they give the cartesian base-change statement. This also constructs the base-changed charts directly. Each original chart is a domain. If the centre is vertical its generic ideal is the unit ideal, so its generic blowup is the identity; its chart rings are torsion-free over \(R\), hence flat by NS1. \(\square\)

#### 2S.3. The node algebra, normality and exact dimension

**NS3.** For an integer \(h\ge1\), set
\[
 A_h=R[x,y]/(xy-\pi^h),\qquad
 \mathfrak m_h=(\pi,x,y).
 \tag{NS5}
\]
This is a flat normal domain. Its local ring at \(\mathfrak m_h\) has dimension two, and is regular exactly when \(h=1\). Away from this special point it is regular and smooth over \(R\). Put also \(A_0=R[x,x^{-1}]\), a smooth chart.

*Proof.* Sending \(y\) to \(\pi^h/x\) embeds \(A_h\) in \(K[x,x^{-1}]\). Reduction of mixed monomials and independence of Laurent monomials prove the unique finite normal form
\[
 a_0+\sum_{i\ge1}a_i x^i+\sum_{j\ge1}b_j y^j,
       \qquad a_i,b_j\in R.
 \tag{NS6}
\]
Thus \(A_h\) is free over \(R\) with the displayed basis.

We prove normality directly. The Laurent ring \(R[z,z^{-1}]\) is integrally closed. In fact its localization \(K[z,z^{-1}]\) is integrally closed: reduce a rational function to coprime numerator and denominator in the Euclidean ring \(K[z]\); a monic integral equation forces the denominator to be a unit after allowing powers of \(z\). Thus an integral element is a Laurent polynomial with coefficients in \(K\). The minimum valuation \(w\) of those coefficients is multiplicative under products: divide each polynomial by the appropriate power of \(\pi\) and reduce modulo \(\pi\), where the product of two nonzero Laurent polynomials is nonzero. If \(w(f)<0\), in a monic equation for \(f\) its highest power has strictly smaller valuation than all other terms, an impossibility. Consequently its coefficients lie in \(R\).

Inside \(K(x)\) we now have
\[
 A_h=R[x,x^{-1}]\cap R[y,y^{-1}],\qquad y=\pi^h/x.
 \tag{NS7}
\]
For the coefficient of \(x^i\), the two membership conditions are \(v(c_i)\ge0\) and \(v(c_i)\ge-hi\). These are exactly (NS6). An element integral over \(A_h\) is integral over each of the two Laurent rings, belongs to both, and hence belongs to \(A_h\).

For dimension, introduce \(s=x+y\). There is an isomorphism
\[
 A_h=R[s,x]/(x^2-sx+\pi^h),
 \tag{NS8}
\]
so this is a finite free integral extension of \(R[s]\). Every prime chain in \(R[s]\) has length at most two. Primes avoiding \(\pi\) correspond to primes in the principal ideal domain \(K[s]\); primes containing it correspond to primes in \(k[s]\). The only possible extra step would require a nonzero prime \(P\subset(\pi)\) avoiding \(\pi\). For \(0\ne f\in P\), divide all its coefficients by their largest common power of \(\pi\). Primality would put the resulting primitive polynomial in \(P\subset(\pi)\), a contradiction.

In an integral extension a strict prime inclusion has strict contraction. To see this, if its contractions both equal \(p\), quotient by the smaller prime and localize the nonzero elements of the base domain modulo \(p\). The resulting integral domain is integral over a field, hence a field: the monic equation of a nonzero element expresses its inverse as a polynomial in it. The purported larger prime cannot then survive; primality shows it does survive if the inclusion was strict. This contradiction proves the claim. It follows from (NS8) that the local dimension is at most two. The chain
\[
 (0)\subsetneq(\pi,x)\subsetneq(\pi,x,y)
 \tag{NS9}
\]
proves that it is exactly two.

For \(h=1\), \(\pi=xy\) and the maximal ideal has the two generators \(x,y\), so the local ring is regular. For \(h>1\), there is no linear relation among \(\pi,x,y\) modulo \(\mathfrak m_h^2\): present the local ring as the quotient of \(R[x,y]_{(\pi,x,y)}\), whose cotangent basis is precisely these three elements, and observe that \(xy-\pi^h\) belongs to the square. Its embedding dimension is three and its dimension is two, so it is not regular. Away from \(\mathfrak m_h\), either the point is generic or \(x\) or \(y\) is invertible. The resulting charts are open parts of a Laurent polynomial ring over \(R\) or \(K\), hence smooth; regularity follows from the flat regular-fibre test proved in Lesson 8, NM2. \(\square\)

#### 2S.4. The three saturated point-blowup charts

**NS4.** For \(h\ge2\), blow up \(\operatorname{Spec}A_h\) in \(\mathfrak m_h\). Its three charts, as subrings of \(K(x)\), are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 B_\pi&=R[a,b]/(ab-\pi^{h-2}),&
       x&=\pi a,& y&=\pi b,\\
 B_x&=R[x,u]/(xu-\pi),&
       u&=\pi/x,& y&=\pi^{h-1}u,\\
 B_y&=R[y,v]/(yv-\pi),&
       v&=\pi/y,& x&=\pi^{h-1}v.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{NS10}
\]
For \(h=2\), interpret \(B_\pi\) as \(R[a,a^{-1}]\).

*Proof.* The generators in NS2 are \(x/\pi,y/\pi\) in the first chart. Their product is \(\pi^{h-2}\); NS3's Laurent normal form proves that there are no other relations. In the \(x\)-chart the generators are \(x,u=\pi/x,y/x\), but
\[
 y/x=\pi^{h-2}u^2,\qquad xu=\pi.
 \tag{NS11}
\]
These show surjectivity of the stated chart map. The same normal-form injection for \(R[x,u]/(xu-\pi)\) into \(K(x)\) proves injectivity. The \(y\)-chart is symmetric.

This cancellation matters. Substitution into the unsaturated equation gives \(\pi^2(ab-\pi^{h-2})=0\) in the first chart and \(x^2(y/x-\pi^{h-2}u^2)=0\) in the second. The graph closure lies in a field, so the indicated factors can and must be cancelled. Retaining them would add components which are not part of the blowup.

On \(B_\pi\cap B_x\), the invertible coordinates satisfy \(a=u^{-1}\), \(x=\pi a\), and \(b=\pi^{h-2}u\). Both overlap rings are \(R[u,u^{-1}]\); the other overlap is symmetric. For \(B_x\cap B_y\) one additionally inverts \(\pi^{h-2}u^2\). The outer charts are regular thickness-one charts. The sole possible remaining nonregular point is the origin in \(B_\pi=A_{h-2}\), and it exists only when \(h-2>1\). The special fibre on every chart is reduced: its equation is a product of two distinct variables, or is the Laurent chart when \(h=2\). \(\square\)

#### 2S.5. Exceptional curves and termination

**NS5.** Repeating NS4 only at the remaining nonregular point takes \(\lfloor h/2\rfloor\) point blowups. The final special fibre replaces the original node by a chain of \(h-1\) copies of \(\mathbf P^1_k\) between the original branches, with \(h\) thickness-one nodes. For \(h=1\) the chain is empty.

*Proof.* For \(h=2\), the exceptional part of \(B_x\) is the affine line \(x=0\), with coordinate \(u\); that of \(B_y\) has coordinate \(v\). The central chart has coordinate \(a\ne0\), and identifies \(u=a^{-1}\) and \(v=a\). This is exactly the two standard affine lines of one projective line. The two original branches meet it at \(u=0\) and \(v=0\), respectively.

For \(h>2\), the exceptional fibre in the central chart consists of the \(a\)-axis and \(b\)-axis. The first glues by \(u=a^{-1}\) to the exceptional affine line of \(B_x\), and the second similarly glues to that of \(B_y\). They are two projective lines, meeting at the central node of thickness \(h-2\); their other ends meet the original branches. Thus the procedure subtracts two from the only unresolved thickness while inserting two end components, until it reaches \(1\), or reaches the final \(2\)-case just described. Induction gives \(h-1\) components and \(h\) edges, and the stated number of blowup rounds.

There is a necessary stopping rule. In the regular chart \(xy=\pi\), the maximal ideal is \((x,y)\). Its \(x\)-blowup chart has \(t=y/x\) and
\[
 R[x,t]/(x^2t-\pi),\qquad
 (R[x,t]/(x^2t-\pi))\otimes_R k=k[x,t]/(x^2t).
 \tag{NS12}
\]
The injection into the fraction field proves this chart identity; equivalently reduce every mixed monomial with \(x^2t=\pi\). The special fibre is not reduced: the nonzero class of \(xt\) is nilpotent. Thus blowing up every special-fibre node, including regular ones, would not prove the assertion. \(\square\)

#### 2S.6. Global resolution and supplied actions

**NS6.** Suppose \(\mathcal C/R\) is integral, flat and projective, with smooth geometrically integral generic curve. Assume its special fibre is split nodal and that it is smooth over \(R\) except at finitely many rational nodes. At each node assume an actual étale neighbourhood with an étale map to an open of \(\operatorname{Spec}A_{h_e}\), taking the node to \(\mathfrak m_{h_e}\), with residue-field identity and with that origin's inverse image equal to the single reduced node after shrinking. These are algebraic chart hypotheses, not merely isomorphisms of completed rings.

Blowing up the reduced union of the total space's nonregular points, and repeating this operation, produces a regular integral flat projective model \(\widetilde{\mathcal C}\) with reduced split nodal special fibre and unchanged generic curve. At most \(\max_e\lfloor h_e/2\rfloor\) rounds are needed. A supplied action on the original model lifts uniquely at every step; a section in its smooth locus lifts uniquely.

*Proof.* NS3 identifies the centre precisely as the nodes with \(h_e>1\). It is a finite reduced closed subscheme, and its coherent ideal is intrinsic. The étale neighbourhoods are flat, so NS2 identifies the blowup there with NS4, because the centre ideal pulls back to the reduced origin ideal.

Here are the local dimension and regularity details. Étale fibres are finite products of separable fields by Lesson 1, EA10. A strict inclusion of primes upstairs cannot have the same contraction: both primes would survive as a strict inclusion in that zero-dimensional fibre. Thus contraction bounds any local prime-chain length by the corresponding length downstairs. Flat going down, proved in EA14, gives the opposite inequality for local faithfully flat maps. Their local dimensions therefore agree. At our residue-identical node the local closed fibre is \(k\), so the base maximal ideal generates the new maximal ideal; flatness identifies its cotangent space with the scalar extension of the base cotangent space. Dimension and embedding dimension are thus exactly those of NS3, so the nonregular points are precisely the stated nodes. At all other points the flat regular-fibre test of NM2 proves regularity on the étale neighbourhoods. The same chain and cotangent argument descends regularity from a surjective étale neighbourhood: both dimensions are preserved, so equality of dimension with embedding dimension descends. This justifies the intrinsic centre used above.

Each step is projective, integral and flat by NS2 and is the identity on the generic fibre and off its finite centre. Every new potential centre is exactly the middle point of NS4. NS5 proves termination, including the bound. The exceptional fibres over a rational node are the actual projective lines just computed: the chosen étale neighbourhood has the same residue field and its fibre over that node is \(\operatorname{Spec}k\), so its exceptional fibre is the same fibre of the blowup. Reducedness and the nodal chart equations also descend along the faithfully flat neighbourhoods. Thus the claimed global fibre has exactly the stated components and intersections. Its regular local rings are normal by Lesson 8, NM1–NM2.

An automorphism, including a supplied semilinear automorphism over \(R\), preserves regularity and hence this reduced centre. NS2 lifts it uniquely. Lifting inverse and composition identities gives an action, rather than a set of unrelated maps. A smooth section avoids every centre and thus lifts through the isomorphism there. This does not extend a generic action which was never supplied on the starting model. \(\square\)

#### 2S.7. Cycles, genera and the actual special-fibre Tate module

**NS7.** Suppose the normalization components of the supplied split nodal fibre are smooth geometrically integral projective curves with genera \(g_v\). Put \(b=\sum_v g_v\), and let \(\Gamma\) be its connected dual graph. Resolution replaces each edge \(e\) by a path of \(h_e\) edges. Its integral cycle lattice is canonically the original one:
\[
 X=H_1(\Gamma,\mathbf Z)
   \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H_1(\widetilde\Gamma,\mathbf Z),
 \qquad (z_e)_e\longmapsto
      (z_e\text{ on every segment of the }e\text{-path}).
 \tag{NS13}
\]
The total component genus \(b\), cycle rank \(r\), and arithmetic genus \(b+r\) are unchanged.

*Proof.* Orient each new path from the old initial vertex to its old terminal vertex. At a new interior vertex the cycle boundary equation forces the two adjacent coefficients to agree. Thus every new cycle is uniquely of the displayed form, and its remaining boundary equations are exactly the old ones, including for loops and multiple edges. This proves the integral isomorphism without tensoring with a field. Each added component is \(\mathbf P^1_k\), whose \(H^1(\mathcal O)\) is zero by PF5's two-chart Laurent computation. The component genus is therefore unchanged. Adding \(h_e-1\) edges and as many vertices leaves \(|E|-|V|+1\) unchanged; NC6's normalization cohomology proves the arithmetic-genus formula. All statements commute with supplied graph actions by their definitions.

There is also a useful exact lattice calculation. On the subdivided graph use the sum of the products of segment coefficients. Under (NS13) it becomes
\[
 Q(z,w)=\sum_e h_e z_e w_e.
 \tag{NS14}
\]
Its positive definiteness follows because all \(h_e>0\); its integral matrix and cokernel can be calculated by PC0. This calculation alone does not identify \(Q\) with a geometric monodromy pairing.

If \(R\) is complete, \(k\) is algebraically closed, and a smooth section and the genus hypotheses of NQ1 are supplied, NS6 now supplies the projective normal model required in NA8. The already proved construction then gives, for \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k\),
\[
 T_\ell G_{\widetilde C}\hookrightarrow
 T_\ell J_C,\qquad
 \operatorname{rank}T_\ell G_{\widetilde C}=2b+r,\qquad
 \operatorname{rank}(T_\ell J_C/T_\ell G_{\widetilde C})=r.
 \tag{NS15}
\]
Here \(G_{\widetilde C}\) is the actual generalized Jacobian constructed in NC1–NC8, and the map is NA8's unique model-torsion lift followed by generic restriction. Its image is saturated and fixed by the absolute Galois group of \(K\). Those properties are NA7–NA8's proved conclusions, not consequences of comparing ranks. No period lattice or equality with all inertia invariants is inferred. \(\square\)

#### 2S.8. Ramification and the remaining model-existence step

**NS8.** Under a finite flat extension of discrete valuation rings \(R\to R'\), write \(\pi=\epsilon\varpi^e\), where \(\epsilon\in(R')^\times\). An old node of thickness \(h\) becomes one of thickness \(eh\):
\[
 xy=\epsilon^h\varpi^{eh}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 x(\epsilon^{-h}y)=\varpi^{eh}.
 \tag{NS16}
\]
When these remain the supplied nodal charts, NS6 applies again. It inserts \(eh-1\) components at that node. Under the canonical cycle identifications, (NS14) is multiplied by \(e\).

*Proof.* The unit change of variable in (NS16) is invertible over \(R'\). The assertion therefore follows directly from NS4–NS7. The length form has one coefficient for each of the \(eh\) unit segments, proving the scaling assertion integrally.

There is no contradiction with flat base change of a fixed blowup. A regular thickness-one node requires no resolution over \(R\); after a ramified extension with \(e>1\), it has thickness \(e\) and does require resolution. The choice of nonregular centre has changed. NS2 commutes a blowup of a specified ideal with flat base change; it does not assert that selecting the new nonregular locus commutes with ramified extension.

NS1 supplies a projective flat model of an embedded smooth generic curve, and NS6 makes an already nodal model regular. The theorem that some finite extension and modification of an arbitrary initial model have the algebraic nodal charts of NS6 is still required. Neither construction assumes that theorem or proves it by calling the starting model semistable. The whole semiabelian lift and the initial analytic period covering in Theorem 2.4 also retain their separate construction requirements. \(\square\)

#### 2S.9. Graded exercise: saturated charts and subdivided cycles

**Exercise 2S (100 points; ten parts of 10 points).** Use NS1–NS8, including their actual chart rings.

1. In \(\mathbf P^2_K\), take \(X_0X_1=\pi^4X_2^2\). Compute the contracted homogeneous ideal over \(R\). Extend the point \([\pi:\pi^3:1]\) to the model. Determine the special-fibre equation and the thickness at \([0:0:1]\).
2. Explain why \(\operatorname{Spec}R[t]/(\pi t)\) is not the flat closure of its generic fibre in \(\mathbf A^1_R\). Compute the actual contracted ideal. Prove the torsion-free flatness assertion needed for that closure.
3. Give the normal form in \(A_5\) of \(x^4y^2+x^2y^3\). For a Laurent polynomial \(\sum c_i x^i\), give the exact coefficient condition for membership in \(A_5\). Test \(x^{-1}\), \(\pi^4x^{-1}\), and \(\pi^5x^{-1}\).
4. Write all three blowup charts for \(h=2\), including the overlap transition between the exceptional \(u\) and \(v\) coordinates. Explain why the exceptional fibre is one projective line rather than two intersecting projective lines.
5. Perform the resolution for \(h=7\). List the successive unresolved thicknesses, the number of rounds, the number of exceptional components and the final number of nodes between the old branches. Locate the two outer regular charts in the first round.
6. In the first central chart for \(h=4\), compare the actual equation with \(\pi^2(ab-\pi^2)=0\). Exhibit the unwanted vertical component of the latter chart, and explain the required saturation. Then compute the special fibre of the blowup of a regular thickness-one node.
7. A connected graph has two vertices and three edges, all oriented from the first vertex to the second. Its component genera are \(1\) and \(2\), and its edge thicknesses are \(1,2,3\). Compute the resolved graph's vertex and edge counts, \(b,r,g\), the cycle basis \(f_1=(1,0,-1)\), \(f_2=(0,1,-1)\), and the matrix and Smith invariants of \(Q\).
8. Repeat the graph and matrix calculations in part 7 after ramification of index two, resolving the new nodes. Compute the order and invariant factors of the matrix cokernel. Explain why this is not yet a computation of a geometric component group.
9. A supplied involution exchanges \(x\) and \(y\) in a thickness-five node. Give its maps on the three first-round charts and describe its action on the final four exceptional components. Explain why the global construction respects the involution even when the residue characteristic is two.
10. Under NS7's complete algebraically closed residue-field hypotheses, compute the ranks in (NS15) for the graph of part 7. For \(\ell=3\), assuming \(\operatorname{char}k\ne3\), compute the orders of the special generalized-Jacobian and generic-Jacobian \(9\)-torsion groups over algebraic closures. State precisely which model-existence and period assertions these rank calculations do not establish.

**Full solution.**

1. The contracted ideal is
   \[
   (X_0X_1-\pi^4X_2^2).
   \tag{NSX1}
   \]
   On monomials reduce every product containing both \(X_0\) and \(X_1\) by their displayed relation. The remaining monomials are independent after passage to \(K\), as is seen by substituting \(X_1=\pi^4X_2^2/X_0\) in the Laurent ring \(K[X_0,X_0^{-1},X_2]\): a fixed pair of Laurent exponents has a unique reduced monomial. The quotient is thus torsion-free over \(R\), so no further element enters the contraction. The given coordinates already lie in \(R\) and \(X_2=1\) is a unit; their equation is \(\pi\pi^3=\pi^4\). The special fibre is \(X_0X_1=0\), two projective lines, meeting at the stated point. On \(X_2=1\) its model equation is \(xy=\pi^4\), so the thickness is \(4\). The section specializes to the node; it is not an example of a section in the smooth locus required for NS6's automatic lift statement.
2. Its generic ideal is \((t)\), whose contraction is still \((t)\). In the proposed larger scheme the nonzero class of \(t\) is killed by \(\pi\), so the ring is not torsion-free. The true closure is \(\operatorname{Spec}R\). For any torsion-free module take the directed collection of finitely generated submodules. Each is free by the DVR module theorem. Tensor products and relations use finitely many elements, so tensoring an injection remains injective in their directed limit, exactly as in NS1. This proves the required flatness.
3. Reduction gives
   \[
   x^4y^2+x^2y^3=\pi^{10}x^2+\pi^{10}y.
   \tag{NSX2}
   \]
   The coefficient condition is \(v(c_i)\ge\max(0,-5i)\). Thus the three proposed elements are respectively outside, outside, and inside; the last is exactly \(y\). Coefficient cancellation is already accounted for by writing the Laurent polynomial uniquely before testing.
4. The charts are
   \[
   R[a,a^{-1}],\qquad R[x,u]/(xu-\pi),\qquad
   R[y,v]/(yv-\pi).
   \tag{NSX3}
   \]
   Their exceptional coordinates satisfy \(u=a^{-1}\), \(v=a\), hence \(uv=1\) on the overlap. The central exceptional chart is \(\mathbf G_{m,k}\), not a pair of axes: its equation is \(ab=1\). Gluing its two ends to the exceptional affine lines gives one \(\mathbf P^1_k\), with the old branches meeting its two distinct endpoints.
5. The unresolved thicknesses are
   \[
   7\longmapsto5\longmapsto3\longmapsto1.
   \tag{NSX4}
   \]
   There are three rounds, six exceptional components, and seven thickness-one nodes. The first outer charts are \(R[x,u]/(xu-\pi)\) with \(y=\pi^6u\), and \(R[y,v]/(yv-\pi)\) with \(x=\pi^6v\). They are already regular. Only the central thickness-five point is blown up in the next round.
6. The actual central equation is \(ab-\pi^2=0\). In the unsaturated quotient the nonzero class of \(ab-\pi^2\) is killed by \(\pi^2\); it is nonzero, for example because mapping \(\pi\) to zero sends it to \(ab\ne0\) in \(k[a,b]\). The whole special fibre of that quotient is the affine plane \(k[a,b]\), instead of the required axes \(k[a,b]/(ab)\). This is an unwanted vertical component. Saturation by powers of \(\pi\) removes it and is forced by the field-subring definition of the blowup chart. For the thickness-one blowup the special fibre is
   \[
   k[x,t]/(x^2t).
   \tag{NSX5}
   \]
   Its element \(xt\) is nonzero but has square zero, and the exceptional component \(x=0\) has multiplicity two. This verifies the stopping rule.
7. The graph has \(6\) edges and \(2+(0+1+2)=5\) vertices. Thus \(r=6-5+1=2\), \(b=3\), and \(g=5\). A cycle \((z_1,z_2,z_3)\) satisfies \(z_1+z_2+z_3=0\), so it is uniquely \(z_1f_1+z_2f_2\), integrally. Repeating its coefficients on the paths gives
   \[
   [Q]_{f_1,f_2}=
      \begin{pmatrix}4&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix},
   \qquad \det Q=11,\qquad
      \operatorname{Smith}(Q)=(1,11).
   \tag{NSX6}
   \]
   The entries have greatest common divisor \(1\); PC0's integer row and column operations therefore give first invariant \(1\), and their product is the determinant \(11\). The added projective lines have genus zero, so they do not change \(b\).
8. The new path lengths are \(2,4,6\). There are \(12\) edges and \(2+(1+3+5)=11\) vertices, again \(r=2\), \(b=3\), \(g=5\). The matrix is
   \[
   \begin{pmatrix}8&6\\6&10\end{pmatrix},\qquad
   \det=44,\qquad
   \operatorname{Smith}=(2,22),\qquad
   \operatorname{coker}\simeq\mathbf Z/2\oplus\mathbf Z/22.
   \tag{NSX7}
   \]
   Its entry gcd is \(2\), and determinant divided by \(2\) is \(22\). These are the cokernel invariants of a specifically computed integral form. Identification with the component group of a geometric model would require a proved geometric pairing and comparison; the matrix computation does not supply them.
9. The central chart \(ab=\pi^3\) has \(a\leftrightarrow b\). The \(x\)-chart maps to the \(y\)-chart by \(x\leftrightarrow y\) and \(u\leftrightarrow v\). These maps respect the overlap ratios in NS4, square to the identity, and exchange the two newly inserted end components. Repeating at the central thickness-three point gives the final reversal
   \[
   (E_1,E_2,E_3,E_4)\longmapsto(E_4,E_3,E_2,E_1).
   \tag{NSX8}
   \]
   The construction uses the invariant centre ideal and uniqueness of the lift, with no division by two or averaging. It therefore works in residue characteristic two as well.
10. The actual special-fibre Tate rank is \(2b+r=8\), the generic Jacobian Tate rank is \(2g=10\), and its saturated free quotient has rank \(2\). Over algebraic closures the prime-to-characteristic torsion orders are
   \[
   |G_{\widetilde C}[9]|=9^8,\qquad
   |J_C[9]|=9^{10}.
   \tag{NSX9}
   \]
   Here the question presupposes residue characteristic different from \(3\). These follow from NC7 and CU9; the quotient of the two orders is \(9^2=81\). They do not construct nodal charts after finite extension for an arbitrary initial curve, extend an unsupplied generic action to a model, construct the whole integral semiabelian group or the analytic period covering, or identify the length form with monodromy. They do give NA8's actual saturated generic submodule once the stated model hypotheses hold.

### 2T. Algebraic charts for a family with split nodal special fibre

This section removes the algebraic-chart hypothesis in §2S when the base is a complete discrete valuation ring and its special-fibre nodes are already split and rational. We begin with the special fibre's completed local equation and construct actual étale maps. The assertion that an arbitrary smooth generic curve acquires a nodal special fibre after finite extension remains a different theorem.

Let \(R\) be a complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizer \(\pi\), fraction field \(K\) and residue field \(k\). A split rational node here means a closed point \(x\) with residue field \(k\), together with the condition
\[
 \widehat{\mathcal O}_{X_k,x}\simeq k[[s,t]]/(st)
 \quad\text{as }k\text{-algebras}.
 \tag{NE1}
\]
The completion is used to recognize the special fibre, not as a substitute for an algebraic neighbourhood. Freely accessible comparison sources are the Stacks project's [nodal-family chart theorem](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CBY), [smooth ambient immersion](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CBL), and [DVR chart formulation](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CDD). We give the local construction below using the already proved completion and invertible-Jacobian results.

#### 2T.1. Embedding the family in a smooth surface

**NE1.** Let \(X/R\) be flat and finitely presented, and let \(x\in X_k\) satisfy (NE1). After shrinking around \(x\), there is a closed immersion
\[
 X=V(g)\subset Y=\operatorname{Spec}B,\qquad
 Y\longrightarrow\mathbf A^2_R
 \text{ étale near }x,
 \tag{NE2}
\]
where \(g\) is a nonzerodivisor. There are étale coordinates \(u,v\) for \(Y/R\), vanishing at \(x\) modulo \(\pi\), for which the reduction of \(g\) has quadratic term \(uv\) and has no constant or linear term at \(x\).

*Proof.* Present an affine neighbourhood of \(X\) as a quotient of \(R[z_1,\ldots,z_n]\). Subtract lifts in \(R\) of its closed-point coordinate values so that the \(z_i\) vanish at \(x\). The dimension of the special-fibre cotangent space is two by (NE1). The relation gradients at \(x\) therefore have rank \(n-2\). Select \(n-2\) actual equations with an invertible \((n-2)\)-row Jacobian minor and let \(Y\) be their common zero scheme, with that determinant inverted. Lesson 3, SF3, and Lesson 1, EA11–EA13, prove directly that the remaining two coordinates give an étale map \(Y\to\mathbf A^2_R\). This defines the required smooth surface and a closed immersion \(X\subset Y\), with a finite ideal \(J\).

Write \(D=\mathcal O_{Y,x}\), let \(J_x\) be that ideal in \(D\), and put \(D_0=D/\pi D\). Flatness of \(X/R\) gives the exact reduction
\[
 0\longrightarrow J_x/\pi J_x
   \longrightarrow D_0\longrightarrow
   \mathcal O_{X_k,x}\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{NE3}
\]
Indeed the only possible left kernel is the \(\pi\)-torsion of \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\), which is zero.

The completion of \(D_0\) is a power-series ring in two variables over \(k\), using the explicit étale-completion calculation of EA11. Its map to (NE1) is onto and induces an isomorphism on cotangent spaces. Choose lifts in the source of the formal coordinates \(s,t\). They have an invertible linear part; substitution is an automorphism of the two-variable power-series ring. To verify this last assertion, solve the inverse linear part, then correct its homogeneous term of degree \(m\) at stage \(m\); later corrections do not change earlier degrees. Completeness gives inverse substitutions in both orders. In these formal coordinates the kernel is exactly the principal ideal generated by their product.

Completion is faithfully flat and exact on finite modules by Lesson 1, EA7, and Lesson 3, DFR1–DFR3. Consequently the finite module \(J_x/\pi J_x\) has one generator at the maximal ideal: its quotient by that maximal ideal is identified with the corresponding one-dimensional quotient of its principal completed ideal. Lift a generator to \(g\in J_x\). Equation (NE3) gives
\[
 J_x=(g)+\pi J_x,
 \tag{NE4}
\]
so Nakayama applied to the finite module \(J_x/(g)\) makes \(J_x=(g)\). Finite generation lets us shrink once more so that \(J=(g)\) on an affine neighbourhood.

The regular local ring \(D\) is a domain by the flat regular-fibre test and NM1–NM2. The element \(g\) is nonzero because its completed reduction generates the nonzero node ideal. Thus it is a nonzerodivisor in \(D\); its annihilator is finite and vanishes on a smaller neighbourhood, so \(g\) is a nonzerodivisor there. The quadratic initial form of its reduction factors as two independent linear forms, by the preceding formal product calculation. Take those two linear combinations of the étale coordinates as \(u,v\), and multiply \(g\) by a unit lifting the inverse of its nonzero quadratic scalar. Their Jacobian determinant is a unit, so they remain étale coordinates. The quadratic term is then \(uv\), as asserted. \(\square\)

#### 2T.2. An algebraic critical section

**NE2.** In NE1's neighbourhood, let \(g_u,g_v\in B\) be the coefficients in
\[
 dg=g_u\,du+g_v\,dv.
 \tag{NE5}
\]
The scheme \(D_{\mathrm{crit}}=V(g_u,g_v)\subset Y\) is étale over \(R\) near \(x\). After shrinking it and \(Y\), it is the image of an actual section \(\sigma:\operatorname{Spec}R\to Y\). Its ideal is \((g_u,g_v)\), and its coordinate ring is \(R\).

*Proof.* The two coefficients are defined by the free differential basis of SF3. Modulo the closed-point ideal, the Jacobian of the map
\[
 Y\longrightarrow\mathbf A^2_R,\qquad
 (u,v)\longmapsto(g_v,g_u)
 \tag{NE6}
\]
is the identity, because the quadratic part of \(g\bmod\pi\) is \(uv\). This statement also holds in characteristic two. To see étaleness without importing a differential criterion, append the two equations prescribing \(g_v,g_u\) to the standard presentation of \(Y\) used in NE1. The enlarged Jacobian is a block matrix; eliminating the original dependent-coordinate block leaves precisely this invertible two-by-two matrix. Its determinant is a unit, so the square-Jacobian theorem EA11–EA13 applies. Taking the fibre over the zero section proves the assertion about \(D_{\mathrm{crit}}\).

Its point over \(x\) has residue field \(k\). EA8's multivariable Hensel proof over the complete ring \(R\) lifts that point uniquely in a pointed square-Jacobian chart to an \(R\)-point. Call the corresponding section \(\sigma\). We explain why an actual open neighbourhood of this section is \(\operatorname{Spec}R\); a formal point alone is not enough.

On an affine étale neighbourhood \(\operatorname{Spec}E\) of the critical point, evaluation at the lifted point gives \(E\to R\). Let \(H\) be its finite kernel. The two maps \(E\to E/H^2\), one the quotient map and one factoring through \(R=E/H\), have the same reduction modulo \(H/H^2\). Formal étaleness makes them equal. Therefore \(H/H^2=0\). At the closed point, \(H\) lies in the maximal ideal; Nakayama gives \(H_x=0\). Kill its finite generators on one principal neighbourhood with denominator \(f\) outside that maximal ideal. Its value \(\sigma(f)\) is a unit of \(R\). Thus
\[
 E_f=R_{\sigma(f)}=R.
 \tag{NE7}
\]
Lift \(f\) to \(B\) and shrink \(Y\) by it. The critical scheme there is precisely this section. \(\square\)

#### 2T.3. Removing the constant and linear terms in actual rings

**NE3.** Put \(U=g_v\), \(V=g_u\), and shrink around the section and its closed point as above. They are étale coordinates, generate its ideal, and there exist \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in B\), with closed-point values \(0,1,0\), and an \(a\in\pi R\), such that
\[
 g= \alpha U^2+\beta UV+\gamma V^2-a.
 \tag{NE8}
\]
If \(X_K\) is a smooth curve, then \(a\ne0\).

*Proof.* By NE2, \(B/(U,V)=R\). Let \(c=\sigma^*(g)\in R\). Since \(g(x)=0\), \(c\in\pi R\). Modulo \((U,V)^2\), write
\[
 g-c\equiv A U+B_1 V,\qquad A,B_1\in R.
 \tag{NE9}
\]
Such an expression exists because \((U,V)/(U,V)^2\) is generated by the indicated classes and its coefficient ring is \(R\). The original expression (NE5) shows that \(dg\) restricts to zero along \(\sigma\). Differentiating (NE9) and restricting to \(\sigma\), the free basis \(dU,dV\) therefore gives \(A=B_1=0\). Thus \(g-c\in(U,V)^2\). Write it as \(\alpha U^2+\beta UV+\gamma V^2\), and set \(a=-c\).

Modulo the closed-point ideal, \(U,V\) have linear terms \(u,v\), respectively. The quadratic term of \(g\) is \(uv\); hence the values of \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) are exactly \(0,1,0\). We may invert \(\beta\) when needed.

If \(a=0\), the entire critical section is contained in \(X=V(g)\). At its generic point the relative differential of \(g\) is zero. The differential presentation therefore gives a two-dimensional tangent space in the smooth surface \(Y_K\), whereas the tangent space of a smooth curve at a rational point has dimension one by SF3. This contradicts the assumed smoothness of \(X_K\). \(\square\)

#### 2T.4. Factoring the quadratic form in every residue characteristic

**NE4.** On the neighbourhood of NE3 take the algebra
\[
 B'=B[\tau]/(\tau^2-\beta\tau+\alpha\gamma),
 \tag{NE10}
\]
localized at \(\tau\), at \(2\tau-\beta\), and at a neighbourhood of the closed point with \(\tau=1\). It is étale over \(B\) at that point and has the same residue field. In \(B'\), set
\[
 p=U+\frac{\gamma}{\tau}V,\qquad
 q=\alpha U+\tau V.
 \tag{NE11}
\]
Then \(g=pq-a\), and \(Y'=\operatorname{Spec}B'\to\mathbf A^2_R\) given by \(p,q\) is étale at that point.

*Proof.* At the closed point the polynomial in (NE10) becomes \(\tau(\tau-1)\). Its derivative at \(\tau=1\) is \(1\), including in characteristic two. The one-equation invertible-Jacobian proof gives an étale neighbourhood there. The defining relation and invertibility of \(\tau\) give
\[
 \tau+\frac{\alpha\gamma}{\tau}=\beta,\qquad
 pq=\alpha U^2+\beta UV+\gamma V^2.
 \tag{NE12}
\]
The product identity follows by multiplying the two linear expressions; no division by two is used. This proves \(g=pq-a\).

At the closed point, \(U=V=\alpha=\gamma=0\) and \(\tau=\beta=1\). All terms differentiating the coefficients in (NE11) are multiplied by \(U\) or \(V\). Therefore
\[
 \left.\frac{\partial(p,q)}{\partial(U,V)}\right|_x
     =\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{NE13}
\]
As in NE2, adjoining the two coordinate-prescription equations to a standard étale presentation gives a square block Jacobian with unit determinant. This proves the claimed actual étale map, rather than only a formal coordinate change. \(\square\)

#### 2T.5. The actual chart and its intrinsic thickness

**NE5.** If \(X_K\) is a smooth curve, there are a pointed étale neighbourhood \(X'\to X\) and an étale \(R\)-map
\[
 X'\longrightarrow
   \operatorname{Spec}R[p,q]/(pq-a),\qquad
 a=\epsilon\pi^h,\quad \epsilon\in R^\times,\quad h\ge1.
 \tag{NE14}
\]
Both maps have residue-field identity at the chosen node. Replacing \(q\) by \(\epsilon^{-1}q\) identifies the target with \(A_h\). The integer \(h\) is independent of all these coordinate choices.

*Proof.* In NE4 take \(X'=V(g)\subset Y'\). Its map to \(X\) is the base change of the étale map \(Y'\to Y\), and its map to \(V(pq-a)\subset\mathbf A^2_R\) is the base change of the just-proved étale coordinate map. They take the selected point to the rational origin. The fibres of these maps at that origin are finite reduced schemes: an étale fibre is finite type, zero-dimensional and a finite product of separable fields by EA10. Remove any other points of these two fibres by shrinking around the chosen point. This supplies exactly the local chart condition of NS6. NE3 gives \(0\ne a\in\pi R\), so its DVR factorization has the stated form.

For invariance, use the actual differential presentation of the nodal hypersurface:
\[
 \Omega_{R[p,q]/(pq-a)\,/R}
   =\big(R[p,q]/(pq-a)\big)^2/
             \big(q\,dp+p\,dq\big).
 \tag{NE15}
\]
The ideal of its first Fitting minors is \((p,q)\), and its quotient is \(R/(a)\). This ideal is intrinsic: presenting a finite module by generators and relations, adding a generator with its defining relation appends an identity block, and elementary row or column operations preserve the ideal of the indicated minors by determinant expansion. Any two finite presentations are related after these operations by adjoining their combined generator list and eliminating the two redundant lists. Hence the Fitting ideal does not depend on the presentation. Invertible scalar extension preserves it by the same determinant formulas; here the étale coordinate changes also identify the relative differential modules, by their lifting property and zero relative differentials.

On the chosen étale neighbourhood, the local critical quotient is an étale \(R/(a)\)-algebra with residue-field identity. Its pointed local factor is exactly \(R/(a)\). To prove this assertion, lift its residue point along successive square-zero layers of the Artinian local ring \(R/(a)\), using EA8; formal étale uniqueness makes the resulting map inverse to the base map. Equivalently the kernel argument of NE2 applies. Its \(R\)-length is thus
\[
 \operatorname{length}_R R/(a)=h.
 \tag{NE16}
\]
The successive classes \(1,\pi,\ldots,\pi^{h-1}\) give \(h\) one-dimensional residue quotients. This length is computed from the intrinsic local differential module of \(X/R\), so every pointed residue-identical chart has the same thickness. \(\square\)

#### 2T.6. From completed special-fibre nodes to regular projective models

**NE6.** Let \(\mathcal C/R\) be integral, flat, finitely presented and projective, with smooth geometrically integral generic curve. Suppose its special fibre is a connected curve smooth away from finitely many split rational nodes in the sense of (NE1). Then \(\mathcal C\) has the algebraic nodal charts required by NS6, and its intrinsic sequence of point blowups gives a regular integral flat projective model with reduced nodal special fibre.

*Proof.* Apply NE1–NE5 separately at the finitely many nodes. Their constructions use affine neighbourhoods of the actual model, not a replacement of its completed surface by a purported algebraic one. At a smooth point of the special fibre, the flat smooth-fibre criterion proved in FQ3's last smoothness paragraph applies. In its actual polynomial presentation, flatness gives the exact fibre ideal sequence. Lift a generating list of that smooth fibre ideal with an invertible gradient minor; Nakayama applied to the residual finite ideal quotient shows that the lifted list generates the whole local ideal. The lifted Jacobian minor is still a unit, so SF3 supplies a smooth chart over \(R\). Thus \(\mathcal C/R\) is smooth there.

There are no additional bad generic points because the generic curve is smooth. We have now proved precisely the hypotheses of NS6, including actual pointed étale charts, so that theorem applies with its proved finite termination bound. Its centres are the nonregular thickness-\(h>1\) nodes. Thickness-one nodes are left alone. Their blowup would have the nonreduced special fibre already calculated in NS12. The construction and all supplied actions are those of NS6. This proves a theorem about an already nodal special fibre, not existence of such a fibre for an arbitrary curve. \(\square\)

#### 2T.7. Lifting a generic point to a smooth section of the resolved model

**NE7.** In NE6, every supplied \(P\in C(K)\) extends uniquely to an \(R\)-section of the original projective model and lifts uniquely through its resolution. Its section on the final regular nodal model lies in the smooth locus.

*Proof.* Embed the given projective model in \(\mathbf P^N_R\). Scale the homogeneous coordinates of \(P\) to have minimum valuation zero. They define an \(R\)-point; its equations vanish because they vanish in \(K\). The diagonal cross-product argument of NS1 proves uniqueness. This works for this actual model, whether or not it was obtained by NS1's particular closure construction.

For each blowup centre ideal \(I\), its pullback to the section is a nonzero ideal of \(R\): generically the centre is empty. It is generated by a power of \(\pi\), hence is an effective Cartier ideal. NS2's universal property supplies a unique lift of the section through the blowup. This argument allows its original specialization to be a singular node.

On the final model a putative nodal specialization has an actual chart \(xy=\pi\), after absorbing a unit. Pull this pointed étale chart back along the section. Completeness of \(R\) and its residue-field identity lift the closed point uniquely to an \(R\)-point of that pullback. At the node both \(x\) and \(y\) have positive valuation; their product has valuation at least two, contradicting \(v(\pi)=1\). Thus the section avoids every node and is in the relative smooth locus. It supplies the root required for NQ and NA once their remaining stated cohomological hypotheses hold. \(\square\)

#### 2T.8. What has and has not been constructed

**NE8.** Under NE6's hypotheses, suppose also that \(k\) is algebraically closed and that the genus and normalization hypotheses in NQ1 and NS7 hold. For \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k\), a supplied generic rational point now yields the actual saturated Tate submodule in NS15 without a separate assumption of algebraic node charts or an original smooth section. All supplied model actions lift as in NS6; no action on a missing model is presumed.

*Proof.* NE6 gives the required projective regular nodal model, and NE7 gives its smooth section. Its regularity implies normality by NM1–NM2. Therefore the actual formal line systems and their projective algebraizations of NQ and NA apply. NC constructs the special generalized Jacobian under its stated normalization hypotheses. NA7's normality argument makes its model-torsion restriction injective, and NA8 constructs and proves saturation of the resulting generic Tate submodule. These are already proved implications, so no new period conclusion is needed.

The remaining general existence step is still to obtain a nodal special fibre after a finite extension and modification for an arbitrary smooth projective generic curve. NE1–NE7 cannot be applied to a cusp or a multiple special component by calling it a split node. The whole integral/formal semiabelian lift, the initial analytic period cover, its exact kernel and local-covering property, and any geometric monodromy-pairing identification remain separate construction requirements. \(\square\)

#### 2T.9. Graded exercise: critical sections and actual node charts

**Exercise 2T (100 points; ten parts of 10 points).**

1. For \(X=\operatorname{Spec}R[x,y,z]/(z-x^2,xy-\pi^3)\), perform NE1's smooth-surface reduction. Give the relevant gradient rank, the ambient étale coordinates, the critical section, the smoothing parameter and the thickness.
2. In \(R[x,y]/(\pi,xy)\), the special fibre is a split node. Show exactly why the flatness step (NE3) fails. Exhibit a nonzero element of its left kernel and explain why this example cannot be used to infer a nodal chart with nonempty smooth generic curve.
3. Let \(g=uv+u^3+v^3-\pi^4\). Compute \(g_u,g_v\), the Jacobian of \((U,V)=(g_v,g_u)\) at the origin and the critical section selected by that point. Determine \(a\). Explain why the construction still works in residue characteristics two and three.
4. In (NE8), take \(\alpha=\pi,\beta=1,\gamma=\pi^2\). Find the root \(\tau\equiv1\bmod\pi\) of its factorization polynomial modulo \(\pi^{10}\), and give the coordinates \(p,q\). Verify their product exactly in the algebra (NE10).
5. For the same example over \(\mathbf F_2[[\pi]]\), give the root modulo \(\pi^{10}\) and the derivative of its defining polynomial. Compare this with the Hessian of \(uv\) in characteristic two. Explain why division by two would invalidate a purported general proof.
6. Compute the local relative differential presentation and its critical quotient for \(xy=\pi^5\). Prove that this family and \(xy=\pi^3\) cannot be related by pointed étale coordinate charts over \(R\) with residue-field identity at their nodes.
7. For \(xy=\pi^5\), start with the section \(x=\pi^2,y=\pi^3\). Follow it through the resolution's two central charts. Show that its final point is smooth, even though the original section passes through a singular point.
8. Take \(R=\mathbf Q[[\pi]]\) and \(y^2=x^3+\pi\). Verify that its affine generic curve is smooth and that its special origin is not a split node. Identify precisely which quadratic and critical-section steps fail if one attempts to use NE1–NE5 there.
9. Over \(\mathbf F_2\), factor \(U^2+UV+V^2\) over \(\mathbf F_4\) using a root \(\omega^2+\omega+1=0\). Deduce an actual node chart for \(U^2+UV+V^2=\pi\) over \(\mathbf F_4[[\pi]]\). Explain the distinction between splitting an already nodal quadratic form and producing a nodal special fibre for an arbitrary curve.
10. Suppose a projective model satisfies NE6, its component genera sum to \(3\), and its dual graph has two vertices joined by three edges of thicknesses \(1,2,5\). Compute the number of simultaneous resolution rounds, exceptional components, final vertices and edges, and the ranks in (NS15), when its additional hypotheses hold. Identify the remaining general model and period obligations.

**Full solution.**

1. The gradient of \(z-x^2\) at the origin has \(z\)-coefficient \(1\); the other equation has no nonzero relative linear coefficient there. The rank is \(1=3-2\). Set \(Y=V(z-x^2)\simeq\mathbf A^2_R\), with coordinates \(x,y\). Its remaining equation is
   \[
   g=xy-\pi^3,\qquad (g_y,g_x)=(x,y),\qquad
   D_{\mathrm{crit}}=\operatorname{Spec}R.
   \tag{NEX1}
   \]
   Thus \(a=\pi^3\) and \(h=3\). Here \(\alpha=\gamma=0,\beta=1\), so \(\tau=1\), \(p=x,q=y\) already give the required algebraic chart.
2. Put \(B=R[x,y]_{(\pi,x,y)}\) and \(J=(\pi,xy)\). In \(J/\pi J\) the class of \(\pi\) is nonzero: if \(\pi\in(\pi^2,\pi xy)\), cancellation in the domain \(B\) gives \(1\in(\pi,xy)\), impossible in this local ring. Its image in \(B/\pi B\) is zero. This is precisely the missing injectivity in (NE3). The quotient is killed by \(\pi\), so it is not flat and its generic fibre is empty. The completed special equation alone does not repair these failures.
3. We have
   \[
   U=u+3v^2,\qquad V=v+3u^2,\qquad
   \frac{\partial(U,V)}{\partial(u,v)}
       =\begin{pmatrix}1&6v\\6u&1\end{pmatrix}.
   \tag{NEX2}
   \]
   Its determinant is \(1\) at the origin. The point \(u=v=0\) is an actual critical section. Hensel uniqueness selects it on the pointed critical neighbourhood, irrespective of any other critical points away from that neighbourhood. Its value of \(g\) is \(-\pi^4\), so \(a=\pi^4\). In characteristic two the off-diagonal derivatives become zero at the origin, and in characteristic three the displayed quadratic corrections disappear; in both cases the determinant remains \(1\). No inversion of \(2\) or \(3\) occurs.
4. Put \(d=\pi^3\). The equation is \(\tau^2-\tau+d=0\), and its root near one is
   \[
   \tau=1-\pi^3-\pi^6-2\pi^9
                  \pmod{\pi^{10}}.
   \tag{NEX3}
   \]
   Substituting the finite polynomial leaves terms of order at least \(12\), so it gives the stated precision. Its derivative \(2\tau-1\) is a unit; completeness and the Newton proof give its unique infinite lift. The actual coordinates are
   \[
   p=U+\frac{\pi^2}{\tau}V,\qquad
   q=\pi U+\tau V,\qquad
   pq=\pi U^2+UV+\pi^2V^2.
   \tag{NEX4}
   \]
   Their cross coefficient is \(\tau+\pi^3/\tau=1\), which follows from the defining polynomial, not from truncating (NEX3).
5. Reduction gives
   \[
   \tau=1+\pi^3+\pi^6\pmod{\pi^{10}},
   \qquad (T^2-T+\pi^3)'=-1=1.
   \tag{NEX5}
   \]
   The Hessian of \(uv\) is
   \[
   \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
   \tag{NEX6}
   \]
   whose determinant is \(1\) in characteristic two. Thus the split cross term has nondegenerate critical equations even in this characteristic. A formula requiring \(1/2\) would not exist in the ring and would not prove the stated theorem.
6. The differential presentation is
   \[
   \Omega_{A_5/R}
      =A_5\,dx\oplus A_5\,dy\big/
                  A_5(y\,dx+x\,dy),\qquad
   A_5/(x,y)=R/(\pi^5).
   \tag{NEX7}
   \]
   Its critical quotient has \(R\)-length \(5\). The analogous quotient for thickness three has length \(3\). The Fitting ideal and the pointed local critical algebra are preserved by étale charts with residue-field identity, by NE5. These two lengths differ, so such charts cannot identify the two pointed families over the same \(R\).
7. In the first central chart,
   \[
   a=x/\pi=\pi,\qquad b=y/\pi=\pi^2,\qquad ab=\pi^3.
   \tag{NEX8}
   \]
   It still specializes to the central node. In the next central chart,
   \[
   a'=a/\pi=1,\qquad b'=b/\pi=\pi,\qquad a'b'=\pi.
   \tag{NEX9}
   \]
   Its specialization has \(a'=1\), so it is outside the node, where both coordinates would vanish. The final point is smooth. This also illustrates the universal-property lift in NE7: each nonzero centre ideal on the section is principal in \(R\).
8. On the generic affine curve the two partial derivatives are \(2y,-3x^2\). They can both vanish only at \(x=y=0\), which does not lie on the generic equation because \(\pi\ne0\). Thus the generic fibre is smooth. At the special origin the quadratic initial term is \(y^2\), a repeated linear factor; it is not the product of two independent linear forms. Its completed cusp ring is therefore not (NE1): an invertible formal coordinate change preserves the quadratic initial form up to an invertible linear substitution and unit scalar. Its critical equations \(2y,-3x^2\) also have noninvertible Jacobian at the origin. Consequently NE2's pointed étale critical section and NE4's coordinate factorization hypotheses are absent. A different finite-extension and modification argument is required.
9. In \(\mathbf F_4\), \(\omega+\omega^2=1\) and \(\omega^3=1\), so
   \[
   U^2+UV+V^2=(U+\omega V)(U+\omega^2V).
   \tag{NEX10}
   \]
   The linear coordinate determinant is \(\omega^2-\omega=1\), a unit. Thus \(p=U+\omega V,q=U+\omega^2V\) give the actual chart \(pq=\pi\) after the displayed unramified coefficient extension. This calculation starts with a nondegenerate nodal quadratic form. It gives no procedure for turning the cusp in part 8, a multiple component, or any arbitrary bad special fibre into a nodal one.
10. The simultaneous number of rounds is
   \[
   \max\{\lfloor1/2\rfloor,\lfloor2/2\rfloor,
                         \lfloor5/2\rfloor\}=2.
   \tag{NEX11}
   \]
   There are \(0+1+4=5\) exceptional projective lines, \(2+5=7\) vertices and \(1+2+5=8\) edges. The cycle rank is \(8-7+1=2\), and the genus is \(3+2=5\). With the additional algebraically closed residue-field, section and cohomological hypotheses of NS7, the special generalized-Jacobian Tate rank is \(2\cdot3+2=8\), the generic Jacobian Tate rank is \(10\), and its saturated free quotient has rank \(2\). This uses the actual line-algebraization and torsion-injection proof of NA8. It does not construct a nodal special fibre after finite extension for an arbitrary curve, the whole integral semiabelian lift, or an analytic period covering and its geometric pairing.

### 2U. Vertical divisors and torsion on a regular model

The next step toward general semistable reduction must deal with a regular model whose special fibre is not yet nodal or reduced. This section constructs the line-bundle obstruction on such a model. Its finite numerical group is defined from actual component degrees; it is not identified with a Néron component group without a further geometric comparison.

Let \(R\) be a complete discrete valuation ring, with uniformizer \(\pi\), fraction field \(K\) and algebraically closed residue field \(k\). Suppose \(X/R\) is an integral regular flat projective relative curve, with smooth geometrically integral generic fibre \(C\). Thus its special-fibre irreducible components \(C_1,\ldots,C_s\) are integral proper curves. The existence of this regular model for an arbitrary \(C\) is not assumed proved by this conditional construction.

The free comparisons are the Stacks project's [vertical-divisor exact sequence](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0C63), [intersection form](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0C66), and [model Picard obstruction](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CAC), together with its [torsion comparison](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CAD) and [specialization injection](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CAE). Every assertion used below has its proof here or in the indicated earlier programme result.

#### 2U.1. Constants, connectedness and component multiplicities

**VP1.** The global functions on \(X\) are exactly \(R\), and the reduced special fibre \(Z=(X_k)_{\mathrm{red}}\) is connected, with \(\Gamma(Z,\mathcal O_Z)=k\). Each \(C_i\) is an effective Cartier divisor and there are positive integers \(m_i\) such that
\[
 \operatorname{div}_X(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^s m_iC_i,
 \qquad
 \mathcal O_X\Big(\sum_i m_iC_i\Big)\simeq\mathcal O_X.
 \tag{VP1}
\]

*Proof.* The finite-complex theorem FC9–FC10 makes \(\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)\) a finite \(R\)-module. Restriction embeds it in \(\Gamma(C,\mathcal O_C)=K\), the proper geometrically integral constants calculation FC20. A finite algebra is integral over its base by the determinant on a finite generating list. The valuation proof DFR7 makes \(R\) integrally closed in \(K\). Hence the global algebra is \(R\).

Idempotents lift uniquely across nilpotent ideals. For a square-zero error \(e^2-e\), replace a tentative lift by \(e-(e^2-e)/(2e-1)\); its derivative is a unit because \((2e-1)^2=1+4(e^2-e)\). Iteration through ideal powers proves existence. If two idempotents differ nilpotently, their difference multiplied by their sum minus one is zero, and the latter is a unit; this proves uniqueness. Local lifts therefore glue.

If \(X_k\) were disconnected, its nontrivial idempotent would consequently give compatible idempotents on every \(X_n=X\times_RR/\pi^{n+1}\). NA1 algebraizes them to an idempotent of \(R\), a contradiction. The same underlying space gives connectedness of \(Z\). Its global functions form a finite reduced \(k\)-algebra: finiteness is proper cohomology, and reducedness follows by restriction to reduced affine charts. Since \(k\) is algebraically closed, such an algebra is a finite product of copies of \(k\). Connectedness leaves one copy.

Regular local rings are factorial and normal by the owned NM1–NM2 proof in Lesson 8. Thus each codimension-one integral component \(C_i\) has a local principal equation, and the ratios of two such equations are units. At its generic point the regular local ring is a DVR; set \(m_i=v_{C_i}(\pi)>0\). Locally factor \(\pi\) in the factorial ring. Its prime factors are exactly the special components through that point, with these exponents. This proves (VP1), including its Cartier statement, and not just an equality of supports. \(\square\)

#### 2U.2. Extending every generic line bundle

**VP2.** Restriction gives the exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathbf Z
   \xrightarrow{\ 1\mapsto m\ }\mathbf Z^s
   \xrightarrow{\ a\mapsto\mathcal O_X(\sum_i a_iC_i)\ }
   \operatorname{Pic}(X)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(C)
   \longrightarrow0,
 \qquad m=(m_1,\ldots,m_s).
 \tag{VP2}
\]
Consequently the group of generically trivial model lines is
\[
 \Lambda=\mathbf Z^s/\mathbf Zm
       \simeq\mathbf Z^{s-1}\oplus\mathbf Z/d,
 \qquad d=\gcd(m_1,\ldots,m_s).
 \tag{VP3}
\]
The displayed decomposition is an abstract group isomorphism, not a chosen equivariant splitting.

*Proof.* Choose a nonzero rational section of a line on the smooth curve \(C\). Its zeros and poles are a finite sum of closed points, by the DVR divisor proof DC1–DC3. The closure of each such point in \(X\) is a codimension-one integral divisor: its prime avoids \(\pi\), and its chains are exactly those in the generic localization. NM2 makes this closure Cartier. The line of the sum of these closures extends the given line on \(C\).

If a model line is generically trivial, use its given generic frame as a rational section on \(X\). Its zero and pole divisors have only vertical components, hence have the form \(\sum a_iC_i\). The local height-one intersection argument NM4 shows that this section identifies the line with \(\mathcal O_X(\sum a_iC_i)\): a quotient of local frames with all height-one valuations zero is a unit, because both it and its inverse belong to every height-one localization.

Finally such a vertical divisor is principal exactly when its coefficient vector is an integer multiple of \(m\). A rational function with this divisor restricts on \(C\) to a function with no zeros or poles. Normality of \(C\) and its constants give an element of \(K^\times\). Write it as \(\pi^a u\), \(a\in\mathbf Z\), \(u\in R^\times\); its divisor is \(a\sum m_iC_i\). This proves exactness of (VP2). PC0's integer Smith reduction applied to the single primitive multiple \(m\) proves (VP3). \(\square\)

#### 2U.3. Actual degrees and the intersection matrix

**VP3.** For a line \(L\) on a proper curve \(D/k\), use
\[
 \deg_D L=\chi(D,L)-\chi(D,\mathcal O_D).
 \tag{VP4}
\]
This degree is additive under tensor products, including on nonreduced curves. The actual component intersection matrix
\[
 Q_{ij}=\deg_{C_i}\mathcal O_X(C_j)|_{C_i}
 \tag{VP5}
\]
is symmetric, has nonnegative off-diagonal entries, and satisfies \(Qm=0\). Moreover, for every model line \(L\),
\[
 \deg_C L|_C=\sum_i m_i\deg_{C_i}L|_{C_i}.
 \tag{VP6}
\]

*Proof.* CE1 makes the product of two line-difference operators zero on sheaves with one-dimensional support. Expanding this product and taking Euler characteristic gives additivity in (VP4). The same result says that a line-difference operator kills every zero-dimensional sheaf class.

If \(i\ne j\), the local equation of \(C_j\) is a nonzerodivisor on the integral curve \(C_i\). Its effective zero scheme is the finite intersection \(C_i\cap C_j\). The section sequence for this Cartier divisor shows
\[
 Q_{ij}
   =\sum_{x\in C_i\cap C_j}
          \operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{X,x}}
                       \mathcal O_{X,x}/(f_i,f_j)
   =Q_{ji}.
 \tag{VP7}
\]
There are no residue-degree factors because the closed points have residue field \(k\). A local line frame does not change the length. The lengths are nonnegative, and are positive exactly when the intersection is nonempty. Restricting (VP1) to each \(C_i\) gives \(Qm=0\), including the diagonal entries.

For completeness, the multiplicity calculation for (VP6) can be made directly in the coherent support filtration. At the generic point of \(C_i\), the local special-fibre module has length \(m_i\) over its DVR. A composition series there has \(m_i\) residue-field quotients. Spread its finitely many generators, maps and equations to an open neighbourhood of that generic point, clearing their finitely many denominators. The resulting finite coherent filtration has \(m_i\) copies of \(\mathcal O_{C_i}\) there. Extend these coherent submodules across the remaining finitely many closed points using the graph-kernel construction in CE1. The discrepancy sheaves then have support dimension zero. Repeating for the finitely many components proves, modulo zero-dimensional sheaf classes,
\[
 [\mathcal O_{X_k}]
       \equiv\sum_i m_i[\mathcal O_{C_i}].
 \tag{VP8}
\]
Apply the line-difference operator for \(L\) and then Euler characteristic. The discrepancy vanishes by CE1. CE3's flat-family Euler theorem equates the degree on \(X_k\) to the degree on \(C\), since \(L\) and \(\mathcal O_X\) are flat over \(R\). This proves (VP6) with its actual multiplicities. \(\square\)

#### 2U.4. The one-dimensional kernel and the finite numerical group

**VP4.** Let \(m^0=m/d\) be the primitive multiplicity vector. Then
\[
 z^{\mathsf t}Qz
   =-\sum_{i<j}Q_{ij}m_im_j
                   \left(\frac{z_i}{m_i}-\frac{z_j}{m_j}\right)^2,
 \qquad
 \ker(Q:\mathbf Q^s\to\mathbf Q^s)=\mathbf Qm.
 \tag{VP9}
\]
The intersection graph is connected, and
\[
 \Phi_X=\ker\big((m^0)^{\mathsf t}:\mathbf Z^s\to\mathbf Z\big)
                     \big/Q\mathbf Z^s
 \tag{VP10}
\]
is a finite group. It is the torsion subgroup of \(\operatorname{coker}Q\). Its order is the product of the nonzero Smith invariants of \(Q\); for \(s=1\) it is the trivial group.

*Proof.* Connectedness of \(Z\) in VP1 makes the intersection graph connected: a partition with no cross intersections would partition its support into two nonempty disjoint closed and open subsets. Use \(Qm=0\) to replace \(Q_{ii}\) by \(-\sum_{j\ne i}Q_{ij}m_j/m_i\). Expansion gives (VP9) term by term. Equality to zero forces \(z_i/m_i=z_j/m_j\) along every edge, hence everywhere. This proves the kernel assertion and \(\operatorname{rank}Q=s-1\).

The map \((m^0)^{\mathsf t}\) is onto \(\mathbf Z\), by the integer Bézout calculation PC0, and kills the image of \(Q\). Thus it gives an exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow\Phi_X\longrightarrow\operatorname{coker}Q
        \xrightarrow{\ (m^0)^{\mathsf t}\ }\mathbf Z
        \longrightarrow0.
 \tag{VP11}
\]
The kernel has rank zero by (VP9), so PC0 makes it finite and identifies it with the torsion subgroup. Smith reduction computes its order. No geometric component-group assertion is needed for this definition.

For \(s>1\) one may also compute the order from cofactors. Every column and row of \(\operatorname{adj}(Q)\) lies in the primitive kernel, so
\[
 \operatorname{adj}(Q)=c\,m^0(m^0)^{\mathsf t},
 \qquad |\Phi_X|=|c|.
 \tag{VP12}
\]
To see that \(c\) is an integer, take an integer vector \(b\) with \(b^{\mathsf t}m^0=1\); then \(c=b^{\mathsf t}\operatorname{adj}(Q)b\). The gcd of the products \(m_i^0m_j^0\) is one, again by Bézout. Consequently the gcd of all \((s-1)\)-minors is \(|c|\), which is the product of the nonzero Smith invariants by PC0. \(\square\)

#### 2U.5. The exact generic torsion obstruction

**VP5.** There is a canonical homomorphism
\[
 \beta:\operatorname{Pic}(C)\longrightarrow\operatorname{coker}Q,
 \qquad
 \beta(\xi)=\big[(\deg_{C_i}L|_{C_i})_i\big],
 \tag{VP13}
\]
where \(L\) is any extension of \(\xi\). Its kernel consists exactly of lines admitting an extension of degree zero on every component. For an integer \(h\ge1\) with \(\gcd(h,d)=1\), there is an exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(X)[h]
    \longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(C)[h]
    \xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }\Phi_X[h].
 \tag{VP14}
\]
No surjectivity at the last group is asserted.

*Proof.* VP2 says that two extensions differ by \(\mathcal O_X(\sum a_iC_i)\), whose degree vector is \(Qa\). Thus (VP13) is independent of the extension. If its class is zero, twist by the inverse of a vertical line with that vector; this gives a componentwise degree-zero extension. The converse is immediate.

A vertical model line of degree zero has coefficient vector \(a\in\ker Q\cap\mathbf Z^s=\mathbf Zm^0\), by VP4 and primitivity. Thus all such lines form the cyclic group generated by
\[
 T=\mathcal O_X\Big(\sum_i m_i^0C_i\Big),\qquad
                       \operatorname{ord}(T)=d.
 \tag{VP15}
\]
Its order is exactly \(d\), not just a divisor, because the vertical group embeds by (VP2). In particular \(\Lambda[h]=0\) when \(\gcd(h,d)=1\), proving injectivity at the first nonzero arrow of (VP14).

For \(\xi\in\operatorname{Pic}(C)[h]\), \(\beta(\xi)\) is torsion, so belongs to \(\Phi_X[h]\) by (VP11). A model torsion line has zero degree on every component and hence maps to zero. Conversely suppose \(\beta(\xi)=0\), and choose a degree-zero extension \(L\). Its power \(L^{\otimes h}\) is a generically trivial degree-zero model line, hence a power of \(T\). Therefore \(L^{\otimes hd}\) is trivial. Choose an integer \(e\) divisible by \(d\) and congruent to \(1\) modulo \(h\), using \(\gcd(h,d)=1\). Then \(L^{\otimes e}\) is killed by \(h\) and restricts to \(\xi\). This proves exactness. Equivalently, one may twist \(L\) by a power of \(T\) using the inverse of \(h\) modulo \(d\). \(\square\)

#### 2U.6. Actual specialization to the reduced fibre

**VP6.** For \(h\) invertible in \(R\), restriction is a canonical isomorphism
\[
 \operatorname{Pic}(X)[h]\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
                         \operatorname{Pic}(Z)[h].
 \tag{VP16}
\]
Its proof uses the projective algebraization theorem NA1–NA4 and does not require a nodal or reduced scheme-theoretic special fibre.

*Proof.* The immersion \(Z\hookrightarrow X_n\) is nilpotent for every \(n\). To verify this on an affine chart, its finitely generated defining radical modulo \(\pi\) is generated by nilpotent elements. A sufficiently large power is contained in \((\pi)\), by the monomial bound in Lesson 1, §6A.2; a further \((n+1)\)-st power vanishes in \(X_n\). Finitely many charts give the claim.

Fix a primitive \(h\)-th root in \(k\). Its unique Hensel lift is a primitive root \(\zeta\in R\); the differences of distinct powers are units. The factorization of \(T^h-1\) and the Chinese remainder calculation identify \(\mu_{h,R}\) with the constant cyclic group \(G=\mathbf Z/h\). A line \(L\) equipped with \(L^{\otimes h}\simeq\mathcal O\) gives a \(G\)-torsor of its compatible frames. Locally its algebra is \(A[T]/(T^h-u)\), \(u\in A^\times\), which is finite free and étale because \(hT^{h-1}\) is a unit. Conversely a \(G\)-torsor gives a line by the character \(1\mapsto\zeta\), with its \(h\)-th tensor power trivial.

Here is the descent in this converse, to keep its scheme content explicit. An étale cover trivializes the torsor; over it take a free rank-one module. On its overlaps multiply by \(\zeta^j\), where the transition element is \(j\in G\). These units satisfy the cocycle, and their \(h\)-th powers equal one. On an affine of the base choose finitely many affine opens in that covering whose images cover it; their disjoint union is affine and faithfully flat.
